name: Canvas
tagline: Institutional learning management system for schools and universities: courses, assignments, gradebook, submissions.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Canvas is sold as institutional contracts priced per enrolled student with multi-year terms, so there is no public monthly number. A free teacher tier exists.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely build you a course site with modules, assignments, due dates and a gradebook in one sitting. That is not what Canvas sells. Canvas sells being the system of record for an institution: roster sync from the student information system, LTI integrations with every textbook publisher and proctoring tool, grade passback, accessibility audits, FERPA posture, single sign on, and an audit trail someone can subpoena. A solo instructor with a free Canvas account gets most of the useful surface for nothing, and a university cannot replace the plumbing with a weekend app no matter how good the UI is. Build the personal study hub if you want one, but do not pretend it is the same category of thing.
coreLoopDIY: A local course workspace where you define modules and assignments, attach files and markdown pages, track due dates on a calendar, and record grades per student in SQLite.
requirements: local file storage for submissions and attachments
no accounts beyond a single admin password if you expose it
whatYouLose: Roster and enrollment sync from an SIS, so every student list is hand maintained forever
The LTI ecosystem: publisher content, proctoring, plagiarism checks, video tools, all of which assume a real LMS on the other end
Single sign on, role based permissions, and the accessibility and FERPA compliance an institution is contractually required to show
Mobile apps students already have installed, plus push notifications and offline grading
Grade passback to the registrar and the legal weight of being the official record
moatNotes: Nobody chooses an LMS, a procurement committee does, and the contract is signed for five years with the SIS integration as the hard dependency.
whyPeopleStillPay: Institutions pay because the LMS is where enrollment, assessment and transcript data meet, and that junction is regulated. A school needs roster sync from its student information system, grade passback to the registrar, accessibility conformance it can document, FERPA handling it can defend, and integrations with whatever publisher platform the textbook adoption committee picked. Replacing that is a procurement project with a legal review, not a software build. Individual instructors mostly do not pay at all: the free teacher tier covers a single course just fine, which tells you the product is aimed at the institution, not the person using it.
notes: The course site is a weekend build; the system of record is not. The moat is SIS roster sync, the LTI integration ecosystem, and a compliance posture a university can show an auditor.
prompt:
Build a single-instructor course workspace that runs entirely on my machine. No cloud, no accounts, no telemetry, no third-party APIs.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, schema created on first boot, file at ./data/course.db
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Uploaded files written to ./data/uploads, served through a route handler, never to a bucket
- Single admin password read from ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, checked by middleware, signed cookie session. Commit a .env.example, never a .env.

Data model:
- courses: title, term, description
- modules: course, title, position
- items: module, type (page | assignment | file), title, body (markdown), position
- assignments: item, due date, points possible, submission type (file | text | none)
- students: course, name, email, optional notes
- submissions: assignment, student, submitted at, text body or stored file path
- grades: assignment, student, score, feedback markdown, graded at

Screens:
1. Course list, create and edit a course.
2. Course home: modules with drag-to-reorder items, inline create of pages and assignments.
3. Page view: markdown rendered with a sanitizer, edit in a plain textarea.
4. Roster: add students one at a time or paste CSV of name,email.
5. Gradebook: students as rows, assignments as columns, editable score cells that save on blur, computed weighted total and letter grade per student.
6. Calendar: month grid of assignment due dates for the selected course.
7. Submissions inbox per assignment: list, open the file or text, enter score and feedback.

Also:
- Export a course to a single JSON file plus the referenced uploads, and import it back.
- Export the gradebook as CSV.
- Seed script that creates one demo course with three modules, four assignments and ten students.

Explicitly out of scope: student logins, multi-tenancy, LTI, SIS or roster sync, SSO, quizzes with question banks, discussion forums, email sending, mobile apps, analytics dashboards.

Finish with a README that says how to run it, where the data lives, and how to back it up by copying ./data.
